Where it began

Jake Weatherald was born in Darwin on 4 November 1994 and grew up there, playing tennis as well as cricket. His cousin Tim Weatherald made his own name in Australian rules football. As a teenager he moved south to Adelaide to pursue the game. His first big chances came with the Northern Territory Strike, for whom he made a hundred against Papua New Guinea in 2013.

In grade cricket he started out keeping wicket for Sturt before moving to Adelaide University. South Australia gave him his first-class debut in February 2016, and he marked it with 58 against New South Wales.

The player

He was an opening batsman who liked to score quickly. In the 2017–18 season he made two hundreds in one Shield match against Western Australia at the WACA, 152 and 143, steering South Australia to a five-wicket win after their hosts had made 514. No South Australian had managed twin hundreds in a Shield game since Darren Lehmann, eighteen seasons before. That same summer he hit 115 from 70 balls in the Big Bash final, the first hundred in a final, as Adelaide Strikers won their first title.

His Test call came for the opening match of the 2025–26 Ashes in Perth. He became only the second man born in the Northern Territory to play for Australia, after Damien Martyn. In the second Test he made 72 from 78 balls. By November 2026 he had played six Tests, scoring 224 runs at 20.36.

What made him special

Big occasions seemed to bring out his best. He made three fifties in a row across two Sheffield Shield finals, and in November 2019 he and Henry Hunt put on 293 for the first wicket, a South Australian record. In the one-day game he once reached a hundred in 66 balls on his way to 141.

His Test debut, it must be said, began quietly: out second ball for nought. He made 22 in the second innings, and half a century in the next match, which is a decent way to answer a quiet start.

Away from the middle

In 2017 he finished second to Hilton Cartwright in the voting for the Bradman Young Cricketer award, after scoring more domestic runs than any other player under 25 in the year counted. Along with South Australia he played for Tasmania and for Hobart Hurricanes, and in 2026 he joined Leicestershire for the first block of the County Championship.

And finally

His bowling was rarely called upon, but he made the most of his chances. In the 2016–17 Shield final he was handed the ball and, in his very first over at that level, bowled Aaron Finch around his legs. Not many part-timers start with a former Australian T20 captain.
